The Wolf UI's dialogs say what will move and what each incident becomes before you confirm.

## Postmortems

**Write postmortem** on a resolved incident creates a **Wolf Postmortem**:

- summary, impact (scope, duration, event count), root cause, lessons;
- action items, each with an owner, a due date and a status;
- a frozen, escaped snapshot of the timeline.

## Metrics

The **Wolf Incident Metrics** script report gives incidents, MTTA (acknowledged − started) and MTTR
(resolved − started): average, p50 and p90 in minutes, per site, bench, host, rule or severity, over
a date range. Merged incidents are left out, so an outage counts once.

## Regulatory reporting

Flag an incident as a **Significant incident (NIS2 Art. 23)**, a **Major ICT-related incident (DORA
Art. 19)** or a **Personal data breach (GDPR Art. 33)** to start its deadlines. They are shown on
the incident, and the **Regulatory deadline** preset alerts before each one. Wolf tracks dates only:
it does not decide what is reportable and sends nothing to an authority. See
[Compliance](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/compliance).

## Public status

Give an incident a **Public Title** to control how it appears on a [status page](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/alerts/status-pages).


# Status pages

A **Wolf Status Page** shows a site's health to guests at `/wolf-status/<slug>`. It is opt-in.

## Create one

| Field                 | Meaning                                                     |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Title**             | Shown at the top of the page.                               |
| **Slug**              | The address: `https://wolf.example.com/wolf-status/<slug>`. |
| **Site**              | The site whose incidents are shown.                         |
| **Bench**             | Optional: also show the bench's incidents.                  |
| **Description**       | Optional text under the title.                              |
| **Show History Days** | How far back resolved incidents are listed.                 |
| **Minimum Severity**  | Incidents below it are not shown.                           |
| **Enabled**           | Until it is ticked, the address answers 404.                |

## What guests see

- An overall banner.
- Open incidents, and those resolved in the last *Show History Days*.
- For each: a title, the severity, a public status (*Investigating*, *Identified*, *Resolved*) and
  the times.

Hosts, rules, summaries and payloads never leave the server.

::caution
Internal titles often name hosts. An incident is shown as "Degraded performance" or "Service
disruption" unless you fill its **Public Title**.
::


# Security overview

Dodock Wolf detects attacks on a Frappe site, its bench and its hosts. It correlates them with
health signals (5xx, failed crons, deployments) in the same incidents. Every security finding is
a **Wolf Event** of type `security` with a `category`, such as `ssh_login_after_failures` or
`permission_change`.

Wolf alone is the baseline. No security feature needs Wazuh or Suricata. When they run on your
hosts, the Wolf Agent reads their alerts too.

## Where each signal comes from

| Source               | Needs                                                 | What it sees                                                                                                                                                                           | Page                                                                                                 |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Wolf site            | the Wolf App installed on the site                    | failed and privileged logins, role grants, Server and Client Scripts, System Console runs, permission changes, weakened System Settings, API keys, Webhooks, data exports, honeytokens | [Site signals](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/site-signals)                          |
| Wolf Agent: nginx    | nginx access logs tailed by the agent                 | probes for secrets, CMS panels, path traversal, injections, scanners; secret files served                                                                                              | [Detection](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/detection)                                |
| Wolf Agent: auth log | `/var/log/auth.log`, `/var/log/secure` or the journal | SSH brute force then login, root logins, sudo failures, new accounts, admin group changes                                                                                              | [Detection](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/detection#host-intrusion-signals)         |
| Wolf Agent: exposure | `/proc/net/tcp{,6}` and `site_config.json`            | bench services listening beyond loopback, development settings in production                                                                                                           | [Detection](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/detection#exposure-and-site-config-risks) |
| Suricata (optional)  | Suricata writing an EVE log on the host               | network IDS alerts (`network_ids_alert`)                                                                                                                                               | [Wazuh and Suricata](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/wazuh-suricata)                  |
| Wazuh (optional)     | a Wazuh manager                                       | host IDS alerts (`hids_alert`)                                                                                                                                                         | [Wazuh and Suricata](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/wazuh-suricata)                  |

Signals that only exist inside a site (logins, scripts, permissions) are captured by the Wolf
App on that site. To see them for every site of a bench, install the app on each one and set
them to satellite mode: see [Every site on a bench](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/install/every-site).

## MITRE ATT\&CK tags

At ingest, every `security` event gets a `mitre_attack` list in its payload: one
`{id, name, tactic}` per technique. Wolf merges the technique mapped to the event's category
with the technique IDs the agent sent. Suricata and Wazuh alerts carry the techniques of the rule
that fired. Events forwarded by satellites keep theirs.

The tags travel with the event to the [SIEM export](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/siem-export): OCSF puts them in
`finding_info.attacks`, CEF in `cs4`.

| Category                                    | Raised by                    | ATT\&CK                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ssh_failed_login`                          | agent (auth)                 | T1110 Brute Force                                                                |
| `ssh_root_login`                            | agent (auth)                 | T1078.003 Local Accounts                                                         |
| `ssh_login_after_failures`                  | agent (auth)                 | T1110, T1078                                                                     |
| `sudo_failure`                              | agent (auth)                 | T1548.003 Sudo and Sudo Caching                                                  |
| `account_created`                           | agent (auth)                 | T1136.001 Create Local Account                                                   |
| `service_account_created`                   | agent (auth)                 | T1136.001 Create Local Account                                                   |
| `admin_group_change`                        | agent (auth)                 | T1098 Account Manipulation                                                       |
| `web_attack_probe`                          | agent (nginx)                | T1595.003, plus the technique of each rule hit (T1190, T1189, T1552, T1595.002…) |
| `web_sensitive_file_exposed`                | agent (nginx)                | T1552.001 Credentials In Files                                                   |
| `service_exposed`, `insecure_site_config`   | agent (exposure)             | T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application                                          |
| `network_ids_alert`                         | agent (Suricata)             | from the rule's `mitre_technique_id` metadata                                    |
| `hids_alert`                                | agent or integration (Wazuh) | from the rule's `rule.mitre.id`                                                  |
| `frappe_failed_login`                       | site                         | T1110                                                                            |
| `new_admin_ip`, `admin_login_new_country`   | site                         | T1078 Valid Accounts                                                             |
| `privileged_user`                           | site                         | T1098                                                                            |
| `server_script_change`, `console_execution` | site                         | T1059.006 Python                                                                 |
| `client_script_change`                      | site                         | T1059.007 JavaScript                                                             |
| `permission_change`                         | site                         | T1098 Account Manipulation                                                       |
| `security_settings_weakened`                | site                         | T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools                                                |
| `api_key_generated`                         | site                         | T1098.001 Additional Cloud Credentials                                           |
| `api_key_new_ip`                            | site                         | T1078 Valid Accounts, T1552 Unsecured Credentials                                |
| `webhook_external`                          | site                         | T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service                                              |
| `data_exfiltration`                         | site                         | T1567, T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits                                           |
| `honeytoken_triggered`                      | site                         | decoy user T1078, T1110; decoy API key T1552; decoy path T1083                   |

## Alerting and response

Each signal has a preset alert rule. Presets are installed with no channels: they open
incidents but notify nobody until you add a channel. See [Presets](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/alerts/presets).

On a security incident, a Wolf Manager can approve a response: block an IP on the host, disable
a user, log out their sessions or revoke their API keys. Nothing runs without that approval. See
[Response actions](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/agent/response-actions).

# Site signals

The site running Dodock Wolf records its own signals from Frappe's documents and requests. No
agent is needed. Each signal has a switch in **Wolf Settings**, and all are on by default.

These signals are only seen from inside a site. To get them for the other sites of a bench,
install the Wolf App on each one in satellite mode: it captures the same signals, with the same
switches, and forwards them to the central site. See [Every site on a bench](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/install/every-site).

## Logins and roles

**Wolf Settings → Local signals (this site)**:

| Setting                                       | Category                  | What it records                                                                                                                                                | Severity                                                   | Preset                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Capture failed logins**                     | `frappe_failed_login`     | a failed desk login (Activity Log), with the user and IP                                                                                                       | warning                                                    | *Repeated failed Frappe logins*: 5+ in 10 min, per site |
| **Flag privileged logins from new IPs**       | `new_admin_ip`            | a privileged user logs in from an IP none of their earlier logins came from                                                                                    | warning                                                    | *Admin login from new IP*                               |
| **Flag privileged logins from new countries** | `admin_login_new_country` | a privileged login from a country none of the user's earlier logins came from. Needs a [GeoIP database](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/#geoip-database) | critical                                                   | *Admin login from new country*                          |
| **Flag users granted privileged roles**       | `privileged_user`         | an enabled user receives a privileged role                                                                                                                     | critical for System Manager or Administrator, else warning | *Privileged role granted*                               |

**Privileged Roles** lists the roles that count as privileged, one per line. Default:
`System Manager`, `Administrator`, `Wolf Manager`.

The same section holds the non-security local signals: **Capture failed Scheduled Job Logs**
(`cron_failure`) and **Capture Error Logs** (failed backups as `backup_failed`). **Watch the Email
Queue** records Email Queue backlogs and sending errors.

## Risky application changes

**Wolf Settings → Flag risky application changes** (on by default) covers:

| Category                     | What raises it                                                                                      | ATT\&CK      | Preset                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `server_script_change`       | a Server Script created, enabled, or with its code, type or trigger changed                         | T1059.006    | *Server Script can run new code* (the event is critical for API and scheduled scripts or guest access) |
| `client_script_change`       | the same for a Client Script                                                                        | T1059.007    | *Client Script can run new code*                                                                       |
| `console_execution`          | each System Console run (Python or SQL)                                                             | T1059.006    | *System Console used*                                                                                  |
| `permission_change`          | see [Permission drift](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/#permission-drift)                     | T1098        | *Permission rules changed*                                                                             |
| `security_settings_weakened` | see [Weakened settings](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/#weakened-settings)                   | T1562.001    | *Security settings weakened* (critical)                                                                |
| `api_key_generated`          | a new API secret written for a user                                                                 | T1098.001    | *API key generated* (the event is critical for privileged users)                                       |
| `api_key_new_ip`             | see [API key used from a new IP](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/#api-key-used-from-a-new-ip) | T1078, T1552 | *API key used from a new IP*                                                                           |
| `webhook_external`           | a Webhook created, enabled or pointed at another host                                               | T1567        | *Webhook to a new host*                                                                                |

Editing a script's description or disabling a script raises nothing.

::caution
Script events keep the first 300 characters of the code. A script that holds a secret puts part
of it in the event.
::

### Permission drift

All of these are `permission_change` events:

- **Role Permission Manager**: add, update, remove and reset. Older Frappe versions write
  `update`, `remove` and `reset` with raw SQL, so Wolf reads them from the request.
- **Custom DocPerm** saved or deleted anywhere else: Data Import, the REST API, code
  (`payload.kind` is `custom_docperm`, `via` says how). Each event lists the rights granted and
  removed. A new rule is compared with the DocType's standard rule, so the copies Frappe makes
  before the first custom change grant nothing. A right given to `Guest` or `All` is critical.
- **User Permission** that lets its user see more (`user_permission`). The first User Permission
  of a user for a DocType only restricts and raises nothing. A further value, an edit that allows
  another value, user or DocType, or removing the last one (which lifts the restriction) raises an
  event.
- **Desk access**: a Website user (customer, supplier portal) given a desk role, which makes them
  a System User (`desk_access`).
- **Role Profile** created or granting more roles.

### Weakened settings

A System Settings save raises `security_settings_weakened` (critical) when it:

- turns off two-factor authentication, the password policy, one session per user, SSO-only login
  or logout on password reset;
- lowers the minimum password score or the lockout duration;
- allows more failed logins, or removes the lockout;
- lengthens sessions;
- lets guests upload files.

### API key used from a new IP

Every successful request authenticated by an API key (`Authorization: token key:secret` or
`Basic`) records the key's address in **Wolf API Key IP**.

- The key's first address, and any address in its first 24 h, form its baseline.
- After that, an address outside every known /24 (IPv4) or /64 (IPv6) raises `api_key_new_ip`,
  critical for privileged users. A new address inside a known network is recorded silently.
- Addresses unused for a year are forgotten. Deleting a row forgets an address.
- The proposed responses are revoking the user's API keys and blocking the address.

### Limits

- Changes made with raw SQL (a patch, `bench mariadb`) fire no document event and are not seen.
  Patches and migrations are skipped on purpose.
- A User Permission restricted to one DocType (`applicable_for`) is counted with the user's
  others for the same allowed DocType.

## Unusual data exports

**Wolf Settings → Flag unusual data exports** (on by default) raises `data_exfiltration`
(T1567, T1030). Preset: *Unusual data export*.

- **What counts**: report exports, Data Export, Data Import templates with records, bulk PDFs,
  and every list read (`frappe.client.get_list`, the list and report views,
  `/api/resource/<DocType>`), whatever the page size. A script paging through a table adds up
  like one big read.
- **How**: the response size of each request counts towards the user's total for the clock
  hour. Every hour, the totals become `user_export_bytes` samples, one series per user
  (`labels.user`).
- **When**: past **Export Floor (MB per hour)** (default `50`), the hour is compared with the
  user's largest hour over the last 14 days. Warning at **Export Factor** (default `5`) times
  that hour, critical at 20 times. A user without any history is critical, except while the site
  itself has less than 14 days of history: then it is a warning.
- **How often**: at most one event per user, hour and severity, so a warning can be followed by
  a critical. The payload has the hour's bytes, requests and rows, the baseline, the ratio, the
  last request and the IP.

::note
The `user_export_bytes` series names users. Anyone who may read the site's metrics in Wolf sees
how much each user took out per hour.
::

Not counted: files sent as they are (private files, backups), printing one document, and the
file of a background list export (its request is counted). An export spread across two clock
hours is split in two. Satellites keep raw samples for 2 days, so their baseline covers 2 days,
not 14.

## GeoIP database

*Admin login from new country* needs an offline GeoIP database on the server. Wolf never calls
an online lookup service.

::steps{level="3"}
### Download a database

Either format works:

- a MaxMind-format `.mmdb` file: GeoLite2-Country or GeoLite2-City (free MaxMind account),
  DB-IP "IP to Country Lite" (`dbip-country-lite-*.mmdb`, CC BY 4.0) or IPinfo Lite. Wolf reads
  it with its own reader, so no extra Python package is needed;
- a CSV of ranges, one per line: `start_ip,end_ip,CC` (DB-IP or IPinfo "country lite" CSV),
  integer `start,end,CC,...` (IP2Location LITE DB1) or `network/prefix,CC`. Header lines are
  skipped.

### Set the path

Set **Wolf Settings → GeoIP Database** to the file's path. A relative path is read from the site
directory, for example `private/files/dbip-country.mmdb`.

### Keep it fresh

Refresh the file monthly. Wolf reloads it when it changes.
::

Private and loopback addresses have no country. A user whose earlier logins all came from such
addresses has no baseline yet, so nothing is flagged until a first public login is known.

## Turning a signal off

Untick its switch in **Wolf Settings**. On a satellite, the same switches apply to the signals it
forwards.


# Web and host detection

The Wolf Agent runs its own web and host detection from logs it already tails. It needs no
Wazuh, Suricata or extra package. All findings are `security` events, scrubbed on the host
before they are sent (see [Scrubbing](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/agent/scrubbing)).

## Web attacks from nginx

The agent reads the same nginx access logs it uses for `http_5xx` and `http_502`. Nothing to turn
on: when the agent tails a bench's nginx log, web attack detection runs. Log paths are set per
bench in `nginx_access_log` (see [Configuration](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/agent/configuration)).

### What counts as a probe

A request is a probe when it:

- looks for secrets: `.env`, `.git/`, `.git-credentials`, `.npmrc`, `docker-compose.yml`,
  `site_config.json`, keys, dumps;
- looks for CMS and admin panels (`wp-login.php`, `phpmyadmin`…);
- looks for edge appliances known for their vulnerabilities: Fortinet, Palo Alto GlobalProtect,
  Ivanti, Citrix, Cisco ASA, F5, Exchange, Confluence and Struts, GeoServer, Jenkins;
- tries path traversal, SQL, command or template injection, or XSS;
- comes from a scanner User-Agent (sqlmap, nuclei, ffuf, dirsearch, katana, LeakIX…).

Appliance paths are matched on the path only and from its root: a DocType, a web page or a query
string may well name Jenkins or Citrix.

Two Frappe rules count only in bursts, since one call is normal: from one client over two minutes,

- 10 calls to the guest endpoints that tell whether an account exists or take a credential
  outside the login page (`frappe_auth_abuse`, `/api/method` and `/api/v2/method`): password reset,
  login link, sign-up, personal data deletion confirmation, the OAuth2 token endpoint (whose
  password grant skipped two-factor authentication before a fix; a refresh token in the URL is
  not counted), LDAP and key or token logins;
- 20 calls to `/api/method`, `/api/resource` or `/api/v2` answered 403, on at least 5 methods
  (`frappe_api_forbidden`): methods tried without the right to call them. 401 is left out: it
  also means an expired session, as after a deploy.

Next to a client's other probes in the same minute, these calls are listed with them. Failed logins on the login page are the site's
own [signal](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/site-signals). A SQL injection in a header or a request body is not in an
access log: [Suricata](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/wazuh-suricata#suricata) sees those.

URL-encoded targets are decoded twice before matching.

### Events

| Category                     | Severity                                         | What it means                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `web_attack_probe`           | warning, critical once a client sends 50+ probes | one event per (site, client) and minute of log time, with the rules hit, the statuses, up to 10 targets and the ATT\&CK IDs |
| `web_sensitive_file_exposed` | critical                                         | a secret-bearing file was answered with a 2xx. The file was probably leaked                                                 |

### What is not a probe

- Attachments (`/files`, `/private/files`) and authorized backup downloads (`/backups`). Static
  assets and attachments are not checked for CMS or appliance names (Font Awesome ships a
  `joomla.svg`).
- A 2xx under a route that answers any sub-path with a page (`/app/`, `/wolf/`, `/api/`…) is not
  counted as a served file.

### The client address

The client is `$remote_addr`. When `$remote_addr` is a loopback or private proxy, the agent takes
the right-most public address of the `X-Forwarded-For` list logged after it: the one your proxy
appended. The left-most entries are written by the client and are not trusted.

### Presets

| Preset                  | Fires when                                                      |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| *Web attack scan*       | 100+ `web_attack_probe` requests in 10 min, per site (warning)  |
| *Sensitive file served* | any `web_sensitive_file_exposed` (critical). Rotate the secrets |

## Host intrusion signals

The agent reads `/var/log/auth.log`, `/var/log/secure`, or the journal:

```bash
journalctl -o short-iso -t sshd -t sshd-session -t sudo -t useradd -t usermod -t gpasswd -t chsh
```

`sshd-session` covers OpenSSH 9.8 and later. The `short-iso` format keeps each line's real
timestamp.

The `auth_log` setting picks the source: `null` auto-detects, a path forces a file, `"journal"`
forces journalctl, `false` turns it off. The installer adds the `wolf-agent` user to the `adm` and
`systemd-journal` groups when they exist, so it can read these logs without root.

| Category                   | What it means                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Severity                              | Preset                                                |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `ssh_failed_login`         | failed SSH logins, aggregated per source IP and minute of log time                                                                                                                                                               | warning, critical at 20+ in one event | *SSH brute force*: 20+ in 10 min, per host (critical) |
| `ssh_root_login`           | a root login                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | warning                               | none                                                  |
| `ssh_login_after_failures` | a successful login from an address that failed 5+ times in the hour before. Failure counts survive push intervals                                                                                                                | critical                              | *SSH login after brute force*                         |
| `sudo_failure`             | wrong sudo passwords, users outside sudoers                                                                                                                                                                                      | warning                               | *Repeated sudo failures*: 3+ in 10 min, per host      |
| `account_created`          | `useradd` creates a local account; or an account is given a login shell (`usermod -s`, `chsh`) or UID 0 (`usermod -u 0`, critical)                                                                                               | warning                               | *New system account*                                  |
| `service_account_created`  | `useradd` creates an account with a system UID (1-999) and no login shell (`/usr/sbin/nologin`, `/sbin/nologin`, `/bin/false`, `/usr/bin/false`, exactly): what a package adds for its service. Recorded, no preset alerts on it | info                                  | —                                                     |
| `admin_group_change`       | a user is added to `sudo`, `wheel`, `admin`, `root`, `adm`, `docker` or `lxd`                                                                                                                                                    | critical                              | *User added to admin group*                           |

::tip
*New system account* fires on planned provisioning too. Open a **Wolf Silence** for the host
while you provision it.
::

## Exposure and site-config risks

Every `exposure.interval` (default 600 s), the agent checks what a host and its sites expose.

### Exposed bench services

`exposed_services` per host counts bench ports listening on all interfaces or on a public address
in `/proc/net/tcp{,6}`:

| Service   | Port                                                          |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| MariaDB   | 3306                                                          |
| Postgres  | 5432                                                          |
| Redis     | 6379, 11000, 12000, 13000, or the bench's own `redis_*` ports |
| socket.io | 9000                                                          |
| gunicorn  | 8000 or `webserver_port`                                      |

Add ports with `exposure.ports`, a map of port to service name. A LAN address is not counted.

::note
A listening socket is not proof of reachability: a firewall may still block what is counted.
::

### Site config risks

`site_config_risks` per site counts these in `site_config.json`:

- `developer_mode`;
- `allow_tests`;
- a plain-HTTP `host_name`;
- `allow_cors: "*"`.

### Events and presets

The agent sends `service_exposed` and `insecure_site_config` events only when the set it finds
changes. Both are tagged T1190.

| Preset                               | Fires when                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| *Bench service exposed*              | `exposed_services` above 0, per host (critical). Redis has no password by default |
| *Development settings in production* | `site_config_risks` above 0, per site (warning)                                   |

Both metrics also feed the [security score](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/compliance#security-score).

## File integrity

Every `integrity.interval` (default 900 s), the agent compares what a bench is made of with its
baseline:

| Watched                                                                                                                                                         | What a change means                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| each app under `apps/<app>/` (not `.git`, `node_modules`, `public/dist` and other `dist`/`build` output, `*.egg-info`, caches, compiled `.pyc` and `.mo` files) | with the app's git commit unchanged: code changed outside a deployment (a web shell, a patched file), **critical**. With a new commit: a deployment, **info**, with both commits, or **warning** when it added Python under a `www/` folder. Without a git checkout (an archive install, an image without `.git`), Wolf cannot tell: **warning**, saying so |
| `sites/common_site_config.json`, each `sites/<site>/site_config.json`                                                                                           | **warning**. Only the names of the keys added, changed or removed are sent, never their values                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| the bench's `config/` (the nginx and supervisor files it generates, not `pids/`), `/etc/nginx` and `/etc/supervisor`                                            | **warning**: someone may have redirected traffic or started a process                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

- Each scan hashes only what changed size or modification time; every `integrity.full_scan_interval`
  (24 h) it hashes everything again, so a file whose size and time were put back is still caught.
- While git holds a lock in an app (a pull or a checkout in progress), the app is judged at the
  next scan, so a deployment is not read as tampering halfway through.
- Files over 32 MB are compared by size and time only, and a pass stops after 200,000 files; what
  is left keeps its baseline until the next pass.
- The first scan of a path is its baseline and raises nothing. The baseline is kept in the spool
  directory (`integrity-state.json`, mode 0600): a restart does not hide what changed meanwhile.
  `wolf-agent check` never moves it. Site config values are kept as HMACs under a key of this
  install (`integrity.key`, 0600).
- A bench or site discovery misses for a while keeps its baseline for 7 days. An app removed from
  `apps/`, a site or a config path that is gone is reported once, as removed (warning).
- A file or folder the agent cannot read keeps its baseline instead of reading as deleted:
  `integrity_unreadable` counts them.
- A site config rewritten with the same keys and values raises nothing.
- Events: `bench_code_changed` (per app) and `bench_config_changed` (per file or server path), with
  up to 20 paths of each kind (added, modified, deleted). Tagged T1505.003 and T1565.001; a
  deployment has no technique. `integrity_files` counts what is watched, per bench and for the
  host's own paths.
- `integrity.server_paths` replaces `/etc/nginx` and `/etc/supervisor`, for example on a host
  whose web server lives elsewhere. The agent's user must be able to read what it watches;
  unreadable files are skipped.

| Preset                                    | Fires when                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| *Bench code changed outside a deployment* | a `bench_code_changed` event at critical, per bench (critical) |
| *Bench or server config changed*          | a `bench_config_changed` event, per host (warning)             |

## Outbound connections

Without Suricata, the agent still notices a bench talking to somewhere new: a light hint of
command-and-control or exfiltration, not packet inspection. Every `outbound.interval` (60 s) it
reads `/proc/net/tcp` and `/proc/net/tcp6` and keeps the established connections that:

- belong to a bench's user, the owner of the bench folder. Knowing which process holds a socket
  would need root, so benches sharing one user share one record, and anything else that user runs
  (an SSH session, a `git push`) counts as the bench's. A bench owned by root is skipped;
- leave from a local port nothing listens on: the bench is the client, not answering a visitor;
- go to a public address. Private, loopback and link-local peers (MariaDB, Redis, a LAN API) are
  left out unless `outbound.include_private`.

A destination is the remote network (/24 for IPv4, /48 for IPv6) and port, so a CDN's next
address is not new. For `outbound.learn_days` (7) after the agent first sees a bench's user, every
destination is learned silently. After that:

- a new destination on an unusual port is reported once as `bench_new_outbound` (**warning**), at
  most 20 per scan; the rest come out at the next scans;
- one on a usual port (web, mail with 2525, IMAP and POP, DNS, NTP, SSH and git, LDAP; add yours
  with `outbound.usual_ports`) is only counted in `bench_new_outbound_usual`, since clouds rotate
  their addresses all day. `outbound.report_usual_ports` reports those too, at **info**.

A destination unseen for 30 days is forgotten. The record is in the spool directory
(`outbound-state.json`, 0600). `bench_outbound_destinations` counts the destinations seen at each
sample.

The event names the destination in `remote_ip` and `remote_port`, not `ip`: a partner the bench
calls is not the remote party of an attack. It is searchable by entity and checked against the
[IP reputation lists](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/journal#ip-reputation-lists), which raise a known-bad
destination, but it never groups incidents by IP, feeds a sequence rule, goes to CrowdSec as an
attacker or gets a block proposal.

**Benches in containers** (Docker, Press, Podman) have their own network. The agent finds them
without root: each container's cgroup names it (`/proc/<pid>/cgroup`), the folder it mounts from
the host (`/proc/<pid>/mountinfo`, for example the bench's `sites/`, on the same filesystem) says
which bench it is, and the container's own TCP table (`/proc/<pid>/net/tcp`) gives its
connections. Several containers of one bench are one record, and a container on the host's
network is not counted twice. The event says `seen_by: container`.

**Behind an outbound proxy**, the connections go to the proxy, not to the real destinations: the
agent reads the proxy's access log instead. `/var/log/squid/access.log` is read when it exists;
`outbound.proxy_logs` sets others (a path, or `[{"path": "...", "format": "squid"}]`); for a
proxy running in a container, give its log's path on the host. Only Squid's native log format is
read. Each request names its destination host and port (`remote_host`), every one of them, not a
sample, and the client address says which bench made it: a container's address, or the host's own
(all its benches). Other clients of a shared proxy, such as machines of the LAN, are left out.
The event says `seen_by: proxy`.

::warning
Squid's log folder is readable by the `proxy` group only on Debian and Ubuntu. The installer adds
the agent's user to it; on a host set up by hand, run `sudo usermod -aG proxy wolf-agent` and
restart the agent. Until then the agent logs that it cannot read the log.
::

**Every new connection, not a sample.** Read from `/proc`, a connection that opened and closed
between two samples is missed: most webhook or API calls last under a second. No kernel interface
lists past connections without root, so this one step is privileged and optional. The helper
`wolf-outbound-log` adds an nftables table that logs every **new** outbound TCP connection of the
bench users (`output`, with their uid) and of the containers behind a Docker, Podman or CNI bridge
(`docker0`, `br-*`, `podman*`, `cni*`; `forward`, with their address). The agent reads those lines
from the kernel log (`journalctl -t kernel`, resuming after a restart, else `/var/log/kern.log`),
runs the helper again when the bench users change, and marks those events `seen_by: kernel`.

```bash [as root]
install -m 0755 -o root -g root agent/wolf-outbound-log.sh /usr/local/sbin/wolf-outbound-log
echo 'wolf-agent ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/sbin/wolf-outbound-log' > /etc/sudoers.d/wolf-outbound-log
chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/wolf-outbound-log
systemctl restart wolf-agent
```

The agent uses it once it is there (`outbound.kernel_log`, `"auto"`). It refuses uid 0.

- Every rule shares one limit: 50 new connections a second for the whole host, so the journal
  cannot be flooded; past it, only what a `/proc` sample sees is counted. UDP (DNS, NTP) is not
  logged, nor are private, loopback and link-local destinations (`outbound.include_private` does
  not apply here).
- Matching new connections turns connection tracking on for the host's traffic.
- Destinations only this log sees get a learning week of their own, from when the helper is first
  applied: installing it on a host learned long ago does not raise a burst of alerts.
- `nft list table inet wolf_outbound` shows the rules and their counters. `"kernel_log": false`
  makes the agent remove the table; to uninstall, run `wolf-outbound-log --off`. Without the
  helper, or when sudo refuses, the agent says so once and keeps sampling `/proc`.

| Preset                         | Fires when                                                                    |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| *Bench connects somewhere new* | a `bench_new_outbound` event at warning (an unusual port), per host (warning) |

## Turning detection off

| To turn off          | Set in the agent config |
| -------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Auth log signals     | `"auth_log": false`     |
| Exposure checks      | `"exposure": false`     |
| File integrity       | `"integrity": false`    |
| Outbound connections | `"outbound": false`     |

Web attack detection follows the nginx logs: it stops for a bench whose nginx log the agent does
not tail.


# Access and secrets

## Roles

Installing the Wolf App creates two roles.

| Role             | Can                                                                               |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Wolf Manager** | see and configure everything, approve response actions, edit Wolf User Scope rows |
| **Wolf User**    | read only. Can comment on incidents. Can be limited with Wolf User Scope          |

System Manager has the same rights as Wolf Manager. The Wolf UI at `/wolf` answers 403 to users
without the Wolf User or Wolf Manager role.

## Wolf User Scope

By default a Wolf User sees every site, bench and host. To limit one, add **Wolf User Scope**
rows at `/app/wolf-user-scope` (Wolf Managers only). One row per grant:

| Field | Value                                 |
| ----- | ------------------------------------- |
| User  | the Wolf User                         |
| Scope | `site`, `bench` or `host`             |
| Value | the name as it appears on Wolf events |

For example:

| User                | Scope | Value           |
| ------------------- | ----- | --------------- |
| <jane@client.com>   | site  | erp.client.com  |
| <jane@client.com>   | site  | shop.client.com |
| <ops-team@dokos.io> | host  | bench-02        |

A restricted user then sees only the Wolf Events, Metric Samples and Rollups, Incidents, Silences
and Agents whose site, bench or host matches one of their rows. This applies in list views,
reports, forms, link searches, the Wolf Overview page, charts and incident timelines.

- Rows are OR-ed.
- Host-wide records (CPU, disk, SSH logins: no site) need a `host` row.
- A Wolf User without any row is not restricted.
- Alert rule definitions stay readable by every Wolf User.

::note
Frappe's own User Permissions cannot do this, because site, bench and host are plain Data fields.
Wolf uses `permission_query_conditions` and `has_permission` hooks instead.
::

## Agent secrets

Each Wolf Agent authenticates with an agent ID and a secret.

- Wolf stores only a salted HMAC-SHA256 hash of the secret.
- The secret is shown once: at registration, or when you click **Rotate secret** on the Wolf
  Agent form.
- Nobody can read it back from the site. To move an agent or recover a lost config, rotate the
  secret or register the host again.

Agents registered before hashing existed keep working: `bench migrate` hashes their stored secret
and deletes the encrypted copy.

A satellite site keeps its own secret encrypted in its Wolf Settings, since it has to send it.
The central site stores only the hash.

**Wolf Settings → Registration Token** is the shared secret that `wolf-agent register --token`
must present. Leave it empty to refuse new registrations. To stop accepting one agent's events,
disable its **Wolf Agent**.

## Push rate limit

Each agent, satellite included, may push at most **Wolf Settings → Max Pushes Per Minute** times
(default `120`, `0` turns the limit off). Excess pushes get HTTP 429. The agent keeps them in its
spool and retries with backoff.

The Wazuh integration endpoint has its own limit of 600 calls per minute, since Wazuh sends one
call per alert. See [Wazuh and Suricata](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/wazuh-suricata#wazuh-integration-route).

Wire details: [Protocol](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/reference/protocol).

## Scrubbing

The agent strips e-mail addresses, credentials, card numbers and IBANs from events before they
leave the host. IP addresses are kept by default, because the security rules group by them. See
[Scrubbing](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/agent/scrubbing).


# Journal and deception

## Tamper-evident journal

Wolf records security-relevant changes in **Wolf Journal Entry** and chains them with an HMAC.
Editing, removing or reordering an entry breaks the chain.

### What is recorded

Each entry is written in the same transaction as the change:

- security events (their payload, as a SHA-256 digest);
- incident decisions: status, owner, merge, the NIS2, DORA and GDPR fields, auto-resolve and
  reopen;
- response actions and their results;
- comments on incidents;
- Wolf Settings changes: the names of the fields changed and who changed them, never the values.

Entries are read-only through Frappe: edits and deletions are refused.

### How it is signed

Every minute, the `chain_journal` job signs the waiting entries in creation order, under a lock:

```text
mac = HMAC-SHA256(key, seq|at|kind|record|digest|prev_mac)
```

An entry waits a minute at most before it is signed.

The key is `wolf_journal_key` in the site config. Wolf creates it on first use and never stores
it in the database, so someone who can only write the database cannot forge a chain.

::warning
Back up `wolf_journal_key` with the site config. Without it, the chain cannot be verified.
::

### Verify the journal

```bash
bench --site wolf.example.com wolf-verify-journal
bench --site wolf.example.com wolf-verify-journal --anchor <seq>:<mac>
```

Or click **Verify** on **Wolf → Security**. Both recompute every digest and mac, and find an
edited, removed or reordered entry.

Deleting the newest entries leaves a valid, shorter chain. To catch that, keep an **anchor**:

::steps{level="4"}
#### Copy the anchor

**Wolf → Security** shows the newest `seq:mac`. **Copy** puts it on the clipboard.

#### Store it where Wolf cannot write

A ticket, a password manager, another server.

#### Check against it

Run `wolf-verify-journal --anchor seq:mac`. A chain cut before that entry fails.
::

::tip
The [SIEM export](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/siem-export) can send every journal entry (seq, digest, mac) to your
collector. That external copy is the best anchor.
::

### Retention

**Wolf Settings → Journal Retention Days** (default `0`: kept forever). With a value set, the
nightly `purge_journal` job removes signed entries older than that, as the oldest part of the
chain:

- it first writes and signs a `journal_purge` entry that records where the purge stopped
  (`through_seq` and its mac), then deletes, under the signing lock;
- it always keeps the newest entry, and never removes an entry the SIEM export has not sent yet
  (when the export sends the journal);
- verification then requires a journal that does not start at entry 1 to start right after the
  newest purge record's cut. Deleting more of the oldest entries, or any without a purge, breaks
  it;
- an anchor in the purged part is reported as purged: copy a newer one. The cut itself still
  verifies, since the purge record keeps its mac.

## Deception: honeytokens

**Wolf Settings → Threat intelligence and deception**. Nobody legitimate knows a honeytoken, so a
single touch raises a critical `honeytoken_triggered` event. The preset *Honeytoken touched*
alerts on it. Each token raises at most one event per address every 10 minutes.

| Setting            | One per line                                                      | Raises an event when                                                              | ATT\&CK      |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| **Decoy users**    | an e-mail of an account nobody uses                               | any login attempt on it, failed or not (Activity Log)                             | T1078, T1110 |
| **Decoy API keys** | an API key, for example one left in an old backup or a repository | any request whose `Authorization` header (`token key:secret` or Basic) carries it | T1552        |
| **Decoy paths**    | a path linked from nowhere, such as `/app/backup-admin`           | any request for it                                                                | T1083        |

The decoy API key check runs before Frappe rejects the unknown key, and commits the event at once.

::caution
Do not create a decoy API key on a real user. The key only needs to appear in the setting.
::

## IP reputation lists

**Wolf Settings → Use IP reputation lists** (off by default).

- Once a day, the `refresh_reputation` job downloads the lists in **IP reputation lists** into
  `private/wolf/ip_reputation.json`.
- Each line of **IP reputation lists** is a name, then a URL or a file path relative to the site.
  Each list holds one address or CIDR per line. Prefilled:
  ```text
  firehol_level1 https://iplists.firehol.org/files/firehol_level1.netset
  spamhaus_drop https://www.spamhaus.org/drop/drop.txt
  ```
- At ingest, a security event whose payload `ip` is on a list gets
  `reputation: {listed, lists}` and one severity step more.
- Lookups never leave the site: only the lists are downloaded. A list that fails to download
  keeps its last copy.

::warning
Check each list's terms of use before enabling it.
::

The CEF format of the [SIEM export](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/siem-export) carries the lists an IP is on in `cs5`.

Wolf can also read the decisions of a CrowdSec Local API (**Wolf Settings → CrowdSec**, off by
default). Events whose IP is under a CrowdSec decision are tagged and raised one step in the same
way. See [Response actions](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/agent/response-actions).


# Compliance and posture

## Regulatory reporting

A **Wolf Incident** has a section *Regulatory reporting (NIS2 / DORA / GDPR)* with three flags.
Each flag starts its own deadlines. The deadlines are shown on the incident, in Desk and in the
Wolf UI. For the rest of the incident workflow, see [Incidents](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/alerts/incidents).

::caution
Wolf tracks dates only. It does not decide whether an incident is significant, major or a
breach, and it sends nothing to an authority.
::

### NIS2 Article 23

Tick **Significant incident (NIS2 Art. 23)**. **Aware since (NIS2)** is set to now; correct it if
you learnt of the incident earlier.

| Obligation                              | Due                                      | Record when sent                  |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Early warning to the CSIRT or authority | 24 h after *Aware since*                 | **Early warning sent at**         |
| Incident notification                   | 72 h after *Aware since*                 | **Incident notification sent at** |
| Final report                            | one month after the notification         | **Final report sent at**          |
| Intermediate report (Art. 23(4)(c))     | the deadline the CSIRT or authority gave | **Intermediate report sent at**   |

- Until the notification is sent, the final report counts from the notification's deadline and
  is marked *estimated*.
- An intermediate report is only due when the CSIRT or the authority asks for one. Record
  **Intermediate report requested at** and, if they gave one, **Intermediate report due by**.
  Without a deadline it is listed "as asked" and never reminded.
- Art. 23(4)(e): while the incident is still open, the report draft reminds you that an ongoing
  incident gets a progress report at the final report's date, and the final report one month
  after it is handled.

### DORA Article 19

For financial entities. Tick **Major ICT-related incident (DORA Art. 19)**. **Aware since (DORA)**
and **Classified as major at** are both set to now; correct them if needed.

The time limits follow Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301, Art. 5:

| Obligation           | Due                                                                                                                                                        | Record when sent                 |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Initial notification | 4 h after *Classified as major*, and no later than 24 h after *Aware since*. A classification made later than those 24 h gives 4 h from the classification | **Initial notification sent at** |
| Intermediate report  | 72 h after the initial notification                                                                                                                        | **Intermediate report sent at**  |
| Final report         | one month after the latest intermediate report                                                                                                             | **Final report sent at**         |

- Until a report is sent, the next one counts from its deadline and is marked *estimated*.
- Record the latest intermediate report: an updated one moves the final report's deadline.
- The weekend and bank holiday extension of Art. 5(4) is not applied. It depends on the entity
  and its Member State, and an earlier deadline is always met.
- DORA reports go through the authority's own templates. The report draft is a starting point.

### GDPR Article 33

Tick **Personal data breach (GDPR Art. 33)**. **Aware since (GDPR)** is set to now. The
notification to the supervisory authority (CNIL in France) is due 72 h after it. Record it in
**Authority notified at**.

### Shared fields

**Authority reference** records the reference the authority gave. It appears in the report draft.

### Deadline alerts

Every 5 minutes, the `check_deadlines` job records one `regulatory_deadline` event per obligation:

- when it is due within 6 h;
- again when it is overdue.

Each event is linked to the incident, so it is on its timeline, with a comment. The
**Regulatory deadline** preset alerts on them (critical).

::warning
Like every preset, *Regulatory deadline* has no channels. Add the channels of whoever reports to
the CSIRT or the CNIL, or the reminders reach nobody. See [Presets](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/alerts/presets).
::

### Report draft

**Regulatory report** (Desk → **Actions**) or **Report draft** (Wolf UI) builds a Markdown draft:

- the facts: incident, scope, severity, status, start and resolution times, authority reference,
  the flags and their dates;
- the deadlines, with what was sent and when;
- the incident summary;
- the postmortem's impact, root cause, lessons and measures, when there is one;
- the timeline: events and comments.

It is a starting point for the authority's form. Check every fact before sending it.

## Security score

**Wolf → Security** (`/wolf/security`) shows a score out of 100 per site, with every check, what
Wolf read and the fix.

| Check                                                                      | Weight | Read from                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Two-factor authentication for System Managers (global switch and the role) | 3      | System Settings and Role: on the Wolf site itself, else the agent's `site_setting`                                     |
| Password policy, minimum score 3                                           | 2      | System Settings (as above)                                                                                             |
| Lockout after 1–10 failed logins                                           | 1      | System Settings (as above)                                                                                             |
| Guests cannot upload files                                                 | 1      | System Settings (as above)                                                                                             |
| No development settings in `site_config.json`                              | 3      | the site config on the Wolf site, else the agent's `site_config_risks`                                                 |
| Bench services not listening beyond loopback                               | 3      | the agent's `exposed_services` on the site's hosts                                                                     |
| A backup newer than 26 h                                                   | 2      | `backup_age_hours`                                                                                                     |
| TLS certificates valid for 14 days or more                                 | 2      | `tls_days_left`                                                                                                        |
| HSTS for 180 days or more, on every domain                                 | 1      | the agent's `hsts_max_age_days`                                                                                        |
| SPF for the mail domain, ending in `-all` or `~all`                        | 1      | DNS, for the domains of the outgoing Email Accounts (Wolf site only)                                                   |
| DMARC policy `quarantine` or `reject`                                      | 1      | DNS, `_dmarc.<domain>`, then its parents' `sp=` / `p=` (Wolf site only)                                                |
| No published security advisory applies to Frappe or ERPNext                | 3      | the agent's `app_version` for the site's benches, and the Wolf site's own packages, against GitHub Security Advisories |

- A check Wolf cannot read is **unknown** and counts as not passed. `coverage` says how much of
  the weight Wolf could read.
- The page lists the failed checks first, then the unknown ones, then the passed ones, the
  heaviest on top in each group. The bar next to the score has one segment per check, as wide as
  its weight: solid for failed and passed, hatched for unknown.
- **+N** on a failed or unknown check is what the score gains if that check alone passes.
- Agent samples older than 3 h are not used.
- The score is stored hourly as the `security_score` metric. The **Security score low** preset
  fires when a site's score is below 60.

### Where the inputs come from

- **System Settings of other sites**: the agent reads them hourly from each site's database, with
  the site's own credentials: five System Settings rows and the System Manager role's two-factor
  flag, nothing else. It uses the `mariadb` / `mysql` client or `psql`. Without a client on the
  host, those checks stay unknown. The Wolf site always reads its own settings.
- **Exposure and site config**: see [Exposure and site-config risks](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/detection#exposure-and-site-config-risks).
- **HSTS**: with the hourly TLS check, the agent sends `HEAD /` and reads
  `Strict-Transport-Security` from the first response. Redirects are not followed. A missing
  header counts as 0 days. No HTTP answer sends no sample, so the check stays unknown.
- **SPF and DMARC**: the Wolf site reads DNS through the resolvers of `/etc/resolv.conf`, for the
  domains of its enabled outgoing Email Accounts, cached 1 h (10 min after a DNS failure, which
  makes the check unknown). SPF needs one `v=spf1` record ending in `-all` or `~all`;
  `redirect=` passes without being followed, `include:` is not followed. DMARC needs
  `p=quarantine` or `p=reject`; `p=none` fails. A subdomain without a record follows its parent's
  `sp=` (else `p=`).
- **Security advisories**: once a day, the Wolf site reads the published advisories of
  `frappe/frappe` and `frappe/erpnext` from the GitHub API, unauthenticated: nothing about the
  installation is sent. A copy older than 7 days is not used. The agent sends `app_version` per
  bench and app hourly; development versions are not sent. Any advisory that applies fails the
  check; the evidence counts them by severity and names the version that fixes them all on that
  line. A major line no advisory of the last year names (Dodock, or a line out of support such as
  13.x) is unknown, never safe. Turn the check off with **Wolf Settings → Check versions against
  GitHub Security Advisories**; it is then unknown.

### Related presets

| Preset                               | Fires when                                      |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| *Security score low*                 | `security_score` below 60, per site (warning)   |
| *Bench service exposed*              | `exposed_services` above 0, per host (critical) |
| *Development settings in production* | `site_config_risks` above 0, per site (warning) |

### Not covered yet

- Advisories of other apps (HRMS, Dokos' own).
- SPF and DMARC of the mail domains of sites other than the Wolf site.


# SIEM export

**Wolf Settings → SIEM export (syslog)** (off by default) sends Wolf's security events and its
signed journal to a syslog collector. Every minute, the events that match the filters, and every
signed journal entry, go out as RFC 5424 syslog (facility `local0`) carrying OCSF JSON or CEF.

## Settings

| Setting                                | Values                                                                                                                 | Default          |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| **Export to a SIEM**                   | on / off                                                                                                               | off              |
| **Collector host**                     | a host name or address. With TLS, it must be in the collector's certificate                                            |                  |
| **Port**                               |                                                                                                                        | `514`            |
| **Transport**                          | `tcp`, `tls` (RFC 5425), `udp` (RFC 5426)                                                                              | `tcp`            |
| **Verify the collector's certificate** | on / off (TLS)                                                                                                         | on               |
| **Collector CA file**                  | a PEM file of a private CA, absolute or relative to the site (`private/files/collector-ca.pem`). Empty: the system CAs |                  |
| **Framing**                            | `octet-counting` or `newline` (TCP and TLS, RFC 6587)                                                                  | `octet-counting` |
| **Message header**                     | `rfc5424` or `none`                                                                                                    | `rfc5424`        |
| **Format**                             | `ocsf` or `cef`                                                                                                        | `ocsf`           |
| **Minimum severity**                   | `info`, `warning`, `critical`                                                                                          | `warning`        |
| **Event types**                        | comma-separated: `security`, `error`, `cron_failure`, `worker_failure`, `host_metric_alert`, `deployment`              | `security`       |
| **Send the journal**                   | also send every signed journal entry (seq, digest, mac)                                                                | on               |

To check a collector, a Wolf Manager can POST to `dodock_wolf.api.siem.send_test`. It sends one
`wolf_test` message with the current settings, even while **Export to a SIEM** is off:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: token <api_key>:<api_secret>" \
  https://wolf.example.com/api/method/dodock_wolf.api.siem.send_test
```

### Format

- **OCSF**: JSON, Detection Finding (class 2004). ATT\&CK techniques in `finding_info.attacks`;
  Wolf's site, bench and payload under `unmapped`. The mapping is Wolf's reading of the schema,
  not a certified profile.
- **CEF**: ATT\&CK in `cs4`, [IP reputation](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/journal#ip-reputation-lists) lists in `cs5`.

### Message header

- `rfc5424`: a syslog header before each message: priority, timestamp, the site as host name,
  `dodock-wolf` as application, the event category as MSGID.
- `none`: the bare JSON or CEF, for collectors that decode the message themselves, such as
  Wazuh's JSON decoder and Graylog's CEF input.

### Transport and framing

- Prefer TCP or TLS. UDP sends one datagram per message, cut at 8 KB. Wolf cannot tell whether
  the collector got anything, so the cursor moves anyway.
- `octet-counting` precedes each message with its length. rsyslog, syslog-ng and Graylog's Syslog
  input read it.
- `newline` sends one message per line; a line break inside a message becomes a space. Wazuh and
  Graylog's CEF input need it.

### TLS

- The collector's certificate is checked against the system CAs, or **Collector CA file**.
- Python 3.13 and later verify strictly: the CA needs `basicConstraints=CA:TRUE` and
  `keyUsage=keyCertSign`, and the server certificate needs an Authority Key Identifier.

::caution
Turning certificate verification off works, but anyone on the path can then read the export.
::

## Delivery

- A cursor moves only after a batch is sent. A collector that is down delays the export; nothing
  is skipped.
- A failure mid-batch can send a message twice: delivery is at least once.
- Events younger than 2 minutes wait for the next run, so a transaction that commits a little
  after it inserted is not skipped.
- Payloads go out as they are stored (already [scrubbed](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/agent/scrubbing) by the agent), cut at
  4 KB.
- Journal entries give the SIEM an external copy of the chain: an anchor Wolf cannot rewrite. See
  [Tamper-evident journal](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/journal#tamper-evident-journal).

## Collectors

Each recipe was tried against the real collector (November 2026).

| Collector                 | Format      | Message header | Transport       | Framing                    | What you get                                                    |
| ------------------------- | ----------- | -------------- | --------------- | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| rsyslog 8.2404            | OCSF or CEF | `rfc5424`      | UDP, TCP or TLS | `octet-counting` (TCP/TLS) | messages written as sent; MSGID is the event category           |
| Wazuh 4.9.2 manager       | OCSF        | `none`         | TCP             | `newline`                  | one Wazuh alert per finding, level by severity                  |
| Graylog 6.1, CEF input    | CEF         | `none`         | TCP             | `newline`                  | every field extracted (source address, ATT\&CK, site, severity) |
| Graylog 6.1, Syslog input | OCSF or CEF | `rfc5424`      | UDP, TCP or TLS | `octet-counting`           | messages stored, JSON not split into fields                     |

::tabs
  :::tabs-item{label="rsyslog"}
  ```text [rsyslog.conf]
  module(load="imptcp")                     # TCP, octet-counted or newline
  input(type="imptcp" port="514")
  module(load="imtcp" StreamDriver.Name="gtls" StreamDriver.Mode="1" StreamDriver.AuthMode="anon")
  input(type="imtcp" port="6514")           # TLS (global DefaultNetstreamDriver* point at the cert)
  module(load="imudp")
  input(type="imudp" port="514")
  ```

  The default Wolf settings work: `rfc5424`, `octet-counting`, OCSF or CEF.
  :::

  :::tabs-item{label="Wazuh"}
  1. On the manager, add a syslog input to `/var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf`:
     ```xml \[ossec.conf]
     <remote>
       <connection>syslog</connection>
       <port>514</port>
       <protocol>tcp</protocol>
       <allowed-ips>WOLF_SITE_ADDRESS/32</allowed-ips>
     </remote>
     ```
  2. Copy the [rules file](https://github.com/bthuner/dodock-wolf/blob/main/docs/siem/wazuh_dodock_wolf_rules.xml){rel=""nofollow""}
     to `/var/ossec/etc/rules/` and restart the manager. It needs Wazuh 4.6 or later.
  3. Set Wolf to: format `ocsf`, message header `none`, transport `tcp`, framing `newline`.

  | Wolf finding  | Wazuh rule | Level |
  | ------------- | ---------- | ----- |
  | info          | 100901     | 3     |
  | warning       | 100902     | 7     |
  | critical      | 100903     | 12    |
  | journal entry | 100910     | 3     |

  The OCSF fields become Wazuh fields: `src_endpoint.ip`, `finding_info.title`,
  `finding_info.attacks`, `unmapped.site`, and so on.

  Does not work with Wazuh:

  - the RFC 5424 header: Wazuh does not parse it, so only a generic rule fires;
  - CEF: Wazuh has no decoder for it;
  - octet-counted frames: they are dropped;
  - TLS: Wazuh's syslog input has none. Put a local relay (rsyslog, stunnel) in front when the
    network between Wolf and Wazuh is not trusted.
  :::

  :::tabs-item{label="Graylog"}
  **To get fields**: create a **CEF TCP** input, then set Wolf to: format `cef`, message header
  `none`, transport `tcp`, framing `newline`.

  - The input extracts `sourceAddress`, `deviceHostName` (the site), `mitre_attack`, `site`,
    `severity`, `event_class_id` (the category) and the journal's `digest` / `mac`.
  - `source` is the address of the Wolf site.
  - The RFC 5424 header confuses this input: `source` becomes `-`.

  **To store only**: the Syslog TCP, UDP or TLS inputs accept the default settings (`rfc5424`,
  `octet-counting`). Graylog keeps MSGID and the structured-data dash at the start of `message`
  and does not split the JSON. Add a JSON extractor or a pipeline rule if you take this road.
  :::

  :::tabs-item{label="UniSOC and others"}
  UniSOC has not been tried, for lack of an instance. Any collector that takes syslog with
  RFC 5424, CEF or JSON lines should work with one of the combinations above.
  :::
::

::note
When Wolf exports to a Wazuh manager that the Wolf Agent also reads, Wazuh's alerts on Wolf's own
export (group `dodock_wolf`) are always left out, so nothing loops back. See
[Wazuh and Suricata](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/wazuh-suricata).
::


# Wazuh and Suricata

Suricata (network IDS) and Wazuh (host IDS) are optional sources. When they run, Wolf reads their
alerts and puts them in the same incidents as its own signals. Wolf never depends on them: without
them, the agent's own [web and host detection](https://bthuner.github.io/dodock-wolf/security/detection) stays on.

| Source   | Event category      | Read by                                                                            | Preset                            |
| -------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Suricata | `network_ids_alert` | the Wolf Agent, from the EVE log                                                   | *Network IDS alert (critical)*    |
| Wazuh    | `hids_alert`        | the Wolf Agent on the manager's host, from `alerts.json`, or the Wazuh integration | *Host intrusion alert (critical)* |

## What each setup covers

With Wolf alone, a bench is covered. Suricata and Wazuh add what a log line cannot show:

|                    | Wolf alone                                                                                                                                                                                                 | + Suricata                                                                                                           | + Wazuh                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Web attacks        | nginx access log: scanners, injections in the URL, CMS and edge appliance paths, secret files (and whether one was served), bursts on Frappe's account endpoints and 403 storms on its API                 | signatures on the traffic itself: request bodies and headers (after TLS termination), every protocol, packet context | the web server's access log through Wazuh's own web attack rules, when its agent reads it                                    |
| Outbound           | new destinations of the bench users and of their containers: sampled from `/proc` every minute; every new TCP connection with the optional `wolf-outbound-log` helper; every request through a Squid proxy | command-and-control signatures, DNS, TLS fingerprints, UDP, the content of the flows                                 | —                                                                                                                            |
| Exposure           | bench services listening beyond loopback, risky `site_config.json` settings                                                                                                                                | the scans and exploits aimed at them                                                                                 | —                                                                                                                            |
| Host               | auth log or journal: SSH brute force then login, root logins, sudo failures, new accounts, admin groups; file integrity of the bench (app code, site configs, nginx and supervisor config)                 | SSH brute force and scans seen on the wire                                                                           | a full HIDS: more log sources, file integrity across the OS, rootkits, configuration assessment, Windows and macOS endpoints |
| Frappe application | logins, roles, Server and Client Scripts, permissions, security settings, API keys, webhooks, exports, honeytokens: only Wolf sees inside a bench                                                          | —                                                                                                                    | —                                                                                                                            |
